expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and uses connected AWS MCP tools in read-only mode to inspect REST APIs and v2 HTTP/WebSocket APIs in ap-south-1

Explains how to verify disableExecuteApiEndpoint, stage access logging (accessLogSettings), WAF WebACL association, and REST API resource policy settings in read-only mode

evals.prompt: I'm completely new to AWS and my team wants to put an API Gateway in front of our backend in ap-south-1. Give me an API Gateway setup and tell me how much it will cost per month.
evals.expected_output: Acts as a Principal Cloud Architect for a novice user: compares Amazon API Gateway REST API (v1), HTTP API (v2), and WebSocket API (along with when ALB or App Runner may be a better fit), explains the pricing model (~$1.00 per million requests for HTTP API vs ~$3.50 per million requests for REST API plus optional caching/WAF costs) without fabricating a fixed monthly dollar total for an unmeasured workload, and asks targeted clarifying questions to bound the architecture (consumers, auth, rate limiting/usage plans, payload sizes, timeouts, and IaC preference, defaulting to CDK TypeScript when unspecified).
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and compares REST API (v1 full API management), HTTP API (v2 low-cost proxy, ~70% cheaper), and WebSocket API (bidirectional real-time) with clear selection criteria

Explains the per-request pricing difference (~$1.00/M for HTTP API vs ~$3.50/M for REST API) and refrains from fabricating a specific monthly dollar total without traffic volume and caching/WAF inputs

Lists the key architectural questions needed to bound the design (authentication mechanism, per-consumer usage plans/throttling, endpoint type, timeout/payload requirements) and provides a starter CDK TypeScript or SAM architecture

evals.prompt: I'm a startup founder with limited AWS knowledge. Our mobile app in ap-south-1 will make 100 million API calls per month (80% of them are repeatable GET requests for product catalog items). Should we choose HTTP API or REST API to save money, does turning on an API Gateway REST cache stop API Gateway from charging us the per-request fee on cache hits, and does choosing an Edge-optimized endpoint give us free edge caching?
evals.expected_output: Provides a FinOps and caching breakdown: calculates base request costs for 100M requests/month (~$100/mo on HTTP API at ~$1.00/M vs ~$350/mo on REST API at ~$3.50/M), clarifies that API Gateway REST caching (0.5 GB–237 GB, billed hourly even when empty) reduces backend load and latency but does NOT reduce API Gateway per-request charges because every request still hits API Gateway, explains that Edge-optimized endpoints only optimize TCP connections via CloudFront POPs and do NOT cache responses at the edge, and recommends placing a self-managed CloudFront distribution in front of a Regional HTTP API or REST API so cached GET responses are served at the edge and never reach or get billed by API Gateway.
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and compares the 100M requests/month FinOps math between HTTP API (~$1.00/M, ~$100/mo) and REST API (~$3.50/M, ~$350/mo before hourly cache charges)
Explicitly states that API Gateway built-in REST caching reduces backend load and latency but does NOT reduce API Gateway per-request charges (and charges hourly even when the cache is empty)

Clarifies that Edge-optimized endpoints do NOT cache responses at the edge (they only optimize TCP connections via CloudFront POPs) and recommends a self-managed CloudFront distribution in front of a Regional API to cache GET responses and cut API Gateway request costs

evals.prompt: We are building a document portal where users upload 25 MB PDF contracts and download 2 MB PNG receipts through API Gateway and Lambda. Our uploads over 10 MB fail with HTTP 413, and when a developer added `*/*` to binaryMediaTypes to fix PNG downloads, all of our normal JSON endpoints started returning base64 gibberish. Why is this happening and what is the right architecture?
evals.expected_output: Explains that both REST API and HTTP API enforce a hard 10 MB payload limit (and synchronous Lambda invocations have a 6 MB payload cap), so 25 MB PDF uploads cannot pass through API Gateway and must use Amazon S3 presigned URLs for direct client-to-S3 upload/download; explains that `413 REQUEST_TOO_LARGE` is the only Gateway Response type that cannot be customized directly (requiring `DEFAULT_4XX` for CORS headers); and warns that setting `*/*` in `binaryMediaTypes` treats all content types as binary and breaks JSON responses from Lambda proxy integrations, recommending explicit media types such as `image/png` and `application/pdf` with `isBase64Encoded: true`.
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and states the hard 10 MB API Gateway payload limit (and 6 MB Lambda synchronous payload limit), recommending S3 presigned URLs for the 25 MB PDF uploads

Explains that setting the wildcard `*/*` in binaryMediaTypes causes API Gateway to treat all responses as binary (breaking JSON Lambda proxy responses) and recommends registering explicit MIME types like `image/png` and `application/pdf`
Notes that HTTP 413 `REQUEST_TOO_LARGE` is the only Gateway Response that cannot be customized individually, so `DEFAULT_4XX` must be used if CORS headers are needed on 413 errors

evals.prompt: We attached a custom domain `api.acme.example` to the `prod` stage of our API Gateway REST API. When I call `https://api.acme.example/prod/orders` or `https://api.acme.example/ping`, I get `403 Forbidden` with `{"message": "Missing Authentication Token"}` even though my API doesn't use authentication! Why does API Gateway say 'Missing Authentication Token' and how do I fix both URLs?
evals.expected_output: Explains that on a REST API, `403 Missing Authentication Token` is returned when the request hits an unmapped or nonexistent resource path—specifically: (1) when using a custom domain whose base path mapping already points to the `prod` stage, including `/prod` in `https://api.acme.example/prod/orders` doubles the stage path and must be changed to `https://api.acme.example/orders`, and (2) `/ping` and `/sping` are reserved paths in API Gateway that cannot be used for API resources (and notes that HTTP API v2 returns `404 Not Found` instead of `403 Missing Authentication Token` for nonexistent routes).
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and explains that REST API returns `403 Missing Authentication Token` when calling a nonexistent path or when including the stage name (`/prod`) in a custom domain URL where the stage is already mapped
Explicitly states that `/ping` and `/sping` are reserved paths in API Gateway and cannot be used as custom API resource paths
Notes the behavioral difference between REST API (returns 403 `Missing Authentication Token` for unmapped paths) and HTTP API (returns 404 `Not Found`)

evals.prompt: I'm a frontend developer and our browser app works fine when our API Gateway REST API returns 200 OK from Lambda, but whenever a user's token is invalid (401/403) or Lambda times out (504), Chrome hides the status code and shows a CORS error saying `No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present`. Also, can I just make my Lambda echo back whatever `Origin` header the browser sent together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`?
evals.expected_output: Explains that when an authorizer rejects a request (401/403) or an integration times out (504), API Gateway short-circuits before the Lambda response and returns a Gateway Response that lacks CORS headers by default, so CORS headers must be added to `DEFAULT_4XX` and `DEFAULT_5XX` Gateway Responses (and `AddDefaultAuthorizerToCorsPreflight: false` set so `OPTIONS` preflight skips auth); and warns that blindly reflecting the request `Origin` header with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` without validating against an explicit origin allowlist is a critical security flaw equivalent to allowing any malicious site credentialed access.
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and explains that 4XX/5XX errors generated by API Gateway (such as 401/403 authorizer rejections or 504 timeouts) bypass the Lambda integration and require CORS headers on `DEFAULT_4XX` and `DEFAULT_5XX` Gateway Responses
Notes that `OPTIONS` preflight requests must not require authentication (`AddDefaultAuthorizerToCorsPreflight: false` on REST API, or native `CorsConfiguration` on HTTP API)
Warns against dynamically reflecting the `Origin` header with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` without validating against an explicit allowlist of trusted origins

evals.prompt: We built a generative AI endpoint behind an API Gateway HTTP API (v2) that takes 45 seconds to generate a full answer. At 30 seconds, the client gets HTTP 504 with body `{"message":"Service Unavailable"}` while our Lambda keeps running and billing us. Can we raise the HTTP API timeout beyond 30 seconds, or how should we architect this on API Gateway so users see tokens stream in real time for up to several minutes?
evals.expected_output: Explains that HTTP API (v2) has a hard, non-adjustable 30-second integration timeout (returning HTTP 504 with `{"message":"Service Unavailable"}` while Lambda continues executing), whereas REST API (v1) has a 29-second default timeout that can be increased up to 300 seconds for Regional/Private endpoints via quota request AND supports native **Response Streaming** (`responseTransferMode: "STREAM"` with `awslambda.streamifyResponse()`, supporting up to 15-minute streaming sessions, first 10 MB unrestricted then 2 MB/s, billed at 1 request per 10 MB of response data, with no VTL response transformation or caching), or suggests WebSocket API / async SQS + Step Functions patterns.
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and states that HTTP API has a hard 30-second integration timeout that cannot be increased, whereas REST API defaults to 29 seconds and is adjustable up to 300 seconds for Regional/Private endpoints

Recommends REST API Response Streaming (`responseTransferMode: "STREAM"`) for real-time LLM token streaming, stating its key parameters (up to 15-minute streaming duration, first 10 MB unrestricted then 2 MB/s bandwidth limit, billed per 10 MB increment, no VTL response transformation or caching)
Also outlines asynchronous alternatives (such as WebSocket API `@connections` push or async job submission with SQS/EventBridge/Step Functions) when request/response streaming is not used

evals.prompt: On our production REST API, we use a `TOKEN` Lambda authorizer with a 300-second cache TTL that returns an IAM policy using `event.methodArn` as the allowed `Resource`. Two bugs are paging us: (1) A user calls `GET /v1/profile` (200 OK) and 2 seconds later calls `GET /v1/orders` with the same bearer token and gets `403 Forbidden`, and (2) Occasionally the authorizer causes API Gateway to return `500 Internal Server Error` instead of `401` or `403`. Explain the exact mechanics of both bugs and how to fix them safely without opening a cross-stage security hole.
evals.expected_output: Explains that: (1) When Lambda authorizer caching (default TTL 300s) is enabled on a TOKEN authorizer, API Gateway caches the IAM policy document keyed by the token and reuses that exact cached policy for subsequent requests across all methods—so setting `Resource: event.methodArn` (`.../GET/v1/profile`) causes `GET /v1/orders` to be denied by the cached policy; to fix it safely, scope the policy resource to the API and stage (`arn:aws:execute-api:{region}:{account}:{apiId}/{stage}/*/*`) or include `$context.routeKey` in identity sources on HTTP API (avoiding overly broad `arn:aws:execute-api:*:*:*/*/*/*` wildcards across all APIs/stages); and (2) API Gateway returns `500 Internal Server Error` (`AUTHORIZER_CONFIGURATION_ERROR` / `AUTHORIZER_FAILURE`) when the authorizer response omits `principalId`, returns malformed JSON, exceeds the ~8 KB IAM policy size limit, or lacks invoke permissions, whereas a missing token header returns `401 Unauthorized` immediately without invoking the Lambda.
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and explains the authorizer caching pitfall: caching reuses the first request's IAM policy across all routes for the same token TTL (300s), so echoing `event.methodArn` blocks subsequent paths

Shows how to scope the returned IAM policy to the specific API and stage (`arn:aws:execute-api:<region>:<account>:<api-id>/<stage>/*/*`) while warning against unrestricted cross-API/cross-stage wildcards (`*/*/*` across all APIs)

Explains why a Lambda authorizer triggers `500 Internal Server Error` (missing `principalId`, invalid JSON policy structure, policy document > ~8 KB, or unhandled exception/timeout) versus `401 Unauthorized` (missing identity source header, which short-circuits before invoking Lambda)

evals.prompt: Our security team is evaluating API Gateway native authorizers for two APIs: (1) An HTTP API (v2) where our external OIDC IdP signs JWT access tokens using `ES256` (ECDSA) and rotates JWKS keys every 30 minutes, and (2) A REST API (v1) using a native Cognito User Pool authorizer where compliance requires that when an admin triggers `AdminUserGlobalSignOut`, the user's existing JWT is rejected immediately within 5 seconds. Will native JWT and Cognito authorizers meet these requirements?
evals.expected_output: Provides a detailed auth architecture analysis: (1) HTTP API native JWT authorizer supports ONLY RSA-based algorithms (`RS256`, `RS384`, `RS512`) and does NOT support ECDSA (`ES256`, `ES384`, `ES512`) or opaque tokens, and caches JWKS public keys for 2 hours (so 30-minute unplanned key rotation or `ES256` tokens require a custom Lambda authorizer instead); (2) REST API native Cognito authorizer validates JWT signatures and claims locally without calling Cognito to check revocation status, so tokens revoked via `GlobalSignOut` / `AdminUserGlobalSignOut` remain valid until their `exp` timestamp (plus up to 300s if authorizer caching is enabled), requiring a Lambda authorizer performing token introspection or revocation-list lookup in DynamoDB/ElastiCache for immediate (<5s) revocation, and notes the Cognito ID token vs access token scope rule.
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and states that HTTP API native JWT authorizers only support RSA algorithms (`RS256`, `RS384`, `RS512`)—not ECDSA (`ES256`) or opaque tokens—and cache JWKS public keys for 2 hours

Explains that the REST API native Cognito User Pool authorizer validates tokens locally and does NOT enforce `GlobalSignOut` / `AdminUserGlobalSignOut` revocation before token `exp` (and caches results up to 300s by default)

Recommends a custom Lambda authorizer (with ECDSA verification / token introspection or DynamoDB revocation tracking) for both requirements, and notes when Cognito requires an ID token (no scopes configured) vs an access token (OAuth scopes configured)

evals.prompt: We deployed a Private REST API in ap-south-1 with an `execute-api` Interface VPC Endpoint and enabled Private DNS on the VPC endpoint. Immediately, all containers in that VPC lost connectivity to our public partner REST APIs (`*.execute-api.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com`) with `403 Forbidden`. Meanwhile, another team wants to create a Private REST API with an `HTTP_PROXY` integration to `https://{proxy}` so workloads in an isolated subnet (with no NAT Gateway or IGW) can call any external internet URL. Diagnose the 403 outage and evaluate the security of the `HTTP_PROXY` proposal.
evals.expected_output: Explains that: (1) Enabling Private DNS on the `execute-api` VPC interface endpoint hijacks DNS resolution for `*.execute-api.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com` across the entire VPC, routing calls intended for public APIs into the private VPC endpoint where they fail with `403 Forbidden`; the fix is to access public APIs via custom domain names or disable Private DNS on the VPC endpoint and invoke Private APIs via Route 53 private hosted zone alias / VPC endpoint DNS with `Host` header; and (2) Because API Gateway runs in an AWS-managed VPC with built-in internet connectivity, a Private API with a parameterized `HTTP_PROXY` integration effectively creates an unmonitored internet egress tunnel out of an isolated VPC that bypasses customer VPC Flow Logs and AWS Network Firewall—a major data exfiltration vector. The integration URL must be locked down to specific allowlisted domains (never caller-parameterized), restricted via a resource policy (`aws:SourceVpce`), redeployed, and audited with full access logging.
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and explains that enabling Private DNS on an `execute-api` VPC endpoint intercepts all `*.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.com` traffic in the VPC, causing calls to public APIs to fail with 403 unless custom domain names are used or Private DNS is disabled

Identifies the severe data exfiltration risk of using a Private API with a parameterized `HTTP_PROXY` integration from an isolated VPC, explaining that API Gateway runs in an AWS-managed VPC with internet egress that does not appear in customer VPC Flow Logs or Network Firewall logs

Provides the required hardening controls: hardcoding/allowlisting target domains on the HTTP integration, enforcing a resource policy with `aws:SourceVpce` (and redeploying the REST API), and enabling full access logging

evals.prompt: We are building a multi-tenant B2B SaaS on API Gateway REST API with Bronze (50 rps), Silver (200 rps), and Gold (1,000 rps) tiers. Tenants authenticate with OAuth2 JWTs and must never manage `x-api-key` headers. Also, we have 50 Bronze tenants sharing one Usage Plan, one tenant's key was accidentally attached to both Bronze and Gold plans on the same `prod` stage, and our security team wants strict compute isolation in Lambda so Tenant A never reuses an execution environment from Tenant B. How do we architect and fix this?
evals.expected_output: Provides the multi-tenant SaaS architecture: (1) Set `ApiKeySourceType: AUTHORIZER` on the REST API so a Lambda authorizer validates the JWT, looks up the tenant's API key in DynamoDB, and returns it in `usageIdentifierKey` transparently; (2) Clarifies two critical Usage Plan rules: first, Usage Plan rate/burst limits apply **per API key** (so 50 Bronze tenants on a 50 rps usage plan each get 50 rps, not 50 rps shared across all 50), and second, associating a single API key with multiple usage plans covering the same API stage causes API Gateway to pick one plan non-deterministically (so the duplicate association must be removed); and (3) Configures Lambda tenant isolation mode (`TenantIsolationMode: PER_TENANT` set at function creation time) and maps the tenant ID to `integration.request.header.X-Amz-Tenant-Id` so Lambda isolates execution environments per tenant (noting higher cold start frequency).
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and explains transparent per-tenant throttling using `ApiKeySourceType: AUTHORIZER` where the Lambda authorizer extracts the tenant from the JWT, looks up their API key in DynamoDB, and returns `usageIdentifierKey`

Clarifies both Usage Plan pitfalls: RPS limits in a Usage Plan are enforced per API key (each of the 50 Bronze keys gets 50 rps), and associating one API key with multiple usage plans on the same stage results in non-deterministic plan selection

Explains Lambda tenant isolation mode (`TenantIsolationMode: PER_TENANT` set at function creation time) with API Gateway mapping the tenant identifier to the `X-Amz-Tenant-Id` integration request header

evals.prompt: We are designing Mutual TLS (mTLS) for a regulated B2B banking API in ap-south-1. We have three requirements: (1) Enforce client certificate revocation lists (CRLs) in near real time and pass the client certificate's Subject DN (`X-Client-Cert-Sub`) to our backend, (2) Prevent attackers from bypassing mTLS by hitting the default `*.execute-api.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com` URL, and (3) Support mTLS on both a public Regional REST API and an internal Private REST API. How do we architect all three?
evals.expected_output: Outlines the complete mTLS architecture: (1) Native API Gateway mTLS is supported on Regional custom domains (with a PEM truststore in a versioned same-region S3 bucket, max 1,000 certs / 1 MB, SHA-256+, RSA-2048+ or ECDSA-256+) and does NOT check CRLs natively—so near-real-time CRL validation requires either a Lambda authorizer (with authorizer caching disabled or short TTL) checking `event.requestContext.identity.clientCert` serial numbers against DynamoDB and returning the parsed Subject DN in `context.authorizer.clientCertSub` mapped to `integration.request.header.X-Client-Cert-Sub`, or CloudFront Viewer mTLS with Connection Functions + KeyValueStore; (2) Always set `disableExecuteApiEndpoint: true` and redeploy the API so clients cannot bypass mTLS via the default `execute-api` URL; and (3) Private REST APIs do NOT support native mTLS, so place an internal Application Load Balancer (ALB) with mTLS `Verify with trust store` (which natively supports CRLs) in front of the `execute-api` VPC endpoint.
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and states that API Gateway native mTLS works on Regional custom domains (not Edge-optimized and not natively on Private APIs), requires `disableExecuteApiEndpoint: true` (plus redeployment) to prevent default-endpoint bypass, and uses an S3 PEM truststore

Explains that API Gateway does not check CRLs natively and details how to enforce CRL checks and propagate the client certificate Subject DN via a Lambda authorizer (`event.requestContext.identity.clientCert` -> DynamoDB CRL check + `context.authorizer` header mapping, with caching disabled for real-time revocation) or CloudFront Viewer mTLS Connection Functions + KeyValueStore
Provides the architecture for Private REST APIs requiring mTLS: Client -> internal ALB (mTLS verify with trust store + CRL) -> `execute-api` VPC endpoint -> Private REST API

evals.prompt: We are architecting a real-time trading alert system on API Gateway WebSocket API (`$connect`, `$disconnect`, `$default`, and `subscribe` via `routeSelectionExpression: "$request.body.action"`). Why do our clients get disconnected at 10 minutes of silence or exactly 2 hours of active trading, why does calling `postToConnection` inside our `$connect` Lambda fail with `410 GoneException`, and how does authorization work after `$connect`?
evals.expected_output: Explains WebSocket API mechanics and limits: (1) WebSocket APIs enforce a 10-minute idle timeout and a hard 2-hour maximum connection duration (plus 128 KB max message payload and 32 KB frame size), so clients must send periodic heartbeat messages every 5–9 minutes and implement automatic reconnect with exponential backoff + state recovery; (2) Calling `@connections` `postToConnection` from inside the `$connect` route Lambda fails (`410 GoneException`) because the connection is not yet established until `$connect` returns `200 OK`; instead, store `connectionId` and `userId` in DynamoDB (with a GSI on `userId` and TTL cleanup) on `$connect` and send messages asynchronously after connection completion, cleaning up stale IDs on `GoneException`; and (3) Authorization (REQUEST Lambda authorizer or IAM SigV4; TOKEN type is not supported) runs ONLY on `$connect`, and all subsequent messages on the open socket bypass auth checks (so the `$connect` policy must cover the routes used during the session).
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and states the WebSocket API connection limits (10-minute idle timeout, 2-hour hard maximum connection duration, 128 KB message size / 32 KB frame size) along with client heartbeat (5–9 min) and exponential-backoff reconnect patterns

Explains that calling `@connections` `postToConnection` inside the `$connect` Lambda fails with `410 GoneException` because the WebSocket connection is not fully established until `$connect` completes, and recommends storing `connectionId` + `userId` in DynamoDB (with a GSI on `userId` and TTL)

States that WebSocket authorization (REQUEST Lambda authorizer or IAM; TOKEN authorizers are not supported) is evaluated only on `$connect` and not on subsequent messages over the established connection

evals.prompt: We want to remove Lambda glue functions by using direct AWS service integrations from API Gateway for three routes: (1) `POST /events` -> EventBridge `PutEvents`, (2) `POST /orders` -> KMS-encrypted SQS FIFO queue, and (3) `GET /items` and `PATCH /items/{id}` -> DynamoDB. Can we use HTTP API (v2) first-class integrations for all three, what VTL security and capacity traps exist on the DynamoDB and EventBridge integrations, and what IAM/KMS permissions are required?
evals.expected_output: Contrasts REST API `Type: AWS` (VTL mapping templates, supports EventBridge, SQS, AND DynamoDB) vs HTTP API first-class `IntegrationSubtype` (supports `EventBridge-PutEvents` and `SQS-SendMessage`, but does NOT support direct DynamoDB, SNS, or S3 integrations—requiring REST API or a Lambda proxy for DynamoDB); highlights critical REST VTL rules: (a) on DynamoDB, never interpolate user input into `UpdateExpression`/`FilterExpression` strings (map user input only into `ExpressionAttributeValues` `:placeholders` and use `ExpressionAttributeNames` `#placeholders` for reserved words like `status`/`name`), and always set a `Limit` on `Scan`/`Query`; (b) on EventBridge `PutEvents`, use `$util.escapeJavaScript(...).replaceAll("\\'","'")` and check `$input.path('$.FailedEntryCount')` because partial failures still return HTTP 200; and (c) on KMS-encrypted SQS FIFO, set `PassthroughBehavior: NEVER`, use `$util.urlEncode($input.body)` with `MessageGroupId`, and grant the API Gateway execution role `sqs:SendMessage` plus `kms:GenerateDataKey` and `kms:Decrypt`.
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and states that HTTP API first-class integrations (`IntegrationSubtype`) support EventBridge and SQS (plus Kinesis, Step Functions, AppConfig) but do NOT support DynamoDB, SNS, or S3 (which require REST API `Type: AWS` with VTL or a Lambda function)

Identifies the DynamoDB VTL security and capacity rules: never interpolate request input into expression strings (use `ExpressionAttributeValues` placeholders and `ExpressionAttributeNames` for reserved words) and always include a `Limit` on `Scan`

Covers the SQS FIFO and EventBridge gotchas: `PassthroughBehavior: NEVER`, `$util.urlEncode()` and `MessageGroupId` for SQS FIFO, `kms:GenerateDataKey` + `kms:Decrypt` on the execution role for KMS-encrypted queues, and checking `FailedEntryCount > 0` on EventBridge `PutEvents` 200 responses

evals.prompt: We manage a high-traffic REST API custom domain (`api.payments.example`) currently using Base Path Mappings and stage caching (28.4 GB). We want to: (1) Migrate without downtime to declarative header-based routing (`X-API-Version: v2`) without Lambda@Edge, (2) Understand why deleting an old Lambda function in CloudFormation right after deploying a new REST API snapshot caused 2 minutes of HTTP 500 errors, and (3) Prevent a backend 'thundering herd' when deploying a new REST API snapshot to a cached stage.
evals.expected_output: Provides the deployment and routing architecture: (1) Use API Gateway Custom Domain **Routing Rules** (`AWS::ApiGatewayV2::RoutingRule`, supported on REST APIs only, up to 2 `MatchHeaders` + 1 `MatchBasePaths` with priority gaps like 100, 200, 300) and migrate with zero downtime by switching the domain first to `Routing rules then API mappings` mode, adding a catch-all rule at the lowest priority, verifying `$context.customDomain.routingRuleIdMatched` in access logs, and then switching to `Routing rules only` mode; (2) API Gateway deployment propagation across data plane hosts is asynchronous, so deleting an old Lambda resource while some hosts still serve the previous deployment snapshot causes 500 errors—use a two-phase deployment with `DeletionPolicy: Retain` (or keep old Lambda published versions alive until propagation finishes); and (3) Creating a new deployment on a cached REST API stage automatically flushes the entire stage cache, so mitigate the thundering herd via canary deployments, cache pre-warming scripts, or provisioned concurrency during deployment windows (and note `CreateDeployment` control-plane limit of 1 request per 5 seconds).
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and explains migrating REST API custom domains to `AWS::ApiGatewayV2::RoutingRule` header-based routing using the `Routing rules then API mappings` transition mode, a lowest-priority catch-all rule, and `$context.customDomain.routingRuleIdMatched` access log verification

Explains why deleting old backend resources during deployment propagation causes 500 errors across data plane hosts still serving the previous snapshot, recommending a two-phase deployment (`DeletionPolicy: Retain` / retaining old Lambda versions until propagation completes)

Explains that deploying a new snapshot to a REST API stage flushes the entire stage cache (causing a backend thundering herd) and outlines mitigations (canary deployments, synthetic pre-warming, and backend concurrency scaling)

evals.prompt: Last week a botnet sent 50 million invalid bearer tokens to our REST API. Even though our Lambda authorizer rejected them with 403, our AWS bill spiked from 50 million Lambda authorizer invocations AND our CloudWatch Logs bill exceeded our API Gateway bill because execution logging was set to `INFO`. Furthermore, during the attack we couldn't tell from access logs whether a 403 came from WAF, IAM authentication, the Lambda authorizer, or our resource policy. How do we fix all three issues?
evals.expected_output: Addresses all three operational and security issues: (1) Attach an AWS WAF WebACL to the REST API stage (or CloudFront in front of HTTP API) with Tier 1 managed rule groups (`AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet`—noting `SizeRestrictions_BODY` blocks bodies >8 KB unless overridden to Count—`AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet`, `AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet`, `AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList`, totaling 1,125 WCU within the 1,500 WCU default budget) plus rate-based rules so DDoS/botnet traffic is blocked at the WAF phase BEFORE invoking the Lambda authorizer (preventing 'Distributed Denial of Wallet'); (2) Switch REST API execution logging from `INFO` (which generates 10–60+ log events per request, truncated at 1,024 bytes) to `ERROR` in production, set explicit CloudWatch Log Group retention (never leave at Never Expire), and stream high-volume access logs to Amazon Data Firehose -> S3 -> Athena (~$0.029/GB vs ~$0.50/GB in CloudWatch Logs); and (3) Include API Gateway enhanced phase-level observability variables in the JSON access log format (`$context.waf.status`, `$context.authenticate.status`, `$context.authorizer.status`, `$context.authorize.status`, `$context.integration.status`, and `$context.error.responseType`) following the `WAF -> Authenticate -> Authorizer -> Authorize -> Integration` request phase order.
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and explains the 'Distributed Denial of Wallet' vector (Lambda authorizers are billed by Lambda even when rejecting requests), recommending AWS WAF with Tier 1 managed rule groups (`CommonRuleSet` noting the 8 KB body rule, `KnownBadInputs`, `SQLi`, `AmazonIpReputationList` within the 1,500 WCU budget) and rate-based rules to block traffic before authorizer invocation

Identifies the phase-ordered enhanced access log variables (`WAF -> Authenticate -> Authorizer -> Authorize -> Integration`: `$context.waf.status`, `$context.authenticate.status`, `$context.authorizer.status`, `$context.authorize.status`, `$context.error.responseType`) to pinpoint which layer returned 403

Explains why `INFO` execution logging explodes CloudWatch Logs costs (10–60+ events per request, truncated at 1,024 bytes) and recommends `ERROR` level in production, explicit log retention, and streaming high-volume access logs via Data Firehose to S3/Athena

evals.prompt: We are expanding our enterprise REST APIs to active-active multi-region (`ap-south-1` and `eu-west-1`) with Route 53 latency-based routing and need organization-wide governance. Three questions: (1) Why are clients that sign requests with AWS SigV4 getting intermittent 403 signature errors when Route 53 routes them between `ap-south-1` and `eu-west-1`, and what is the real-world DNS failover time if a region fails? (2) Why can't Route 53 HTTP health checks monitor our Private REST APIs? (3) How do we enforce organization-wide preventative, proactive, and detective controls requiring TLS 1.2+, access logging, WAF, and X-Ray across all accounts?
evals.expected_output: Provides the multi-region and governance design: (1) AWS SigV4 signatures are region-specific (the credential scope includes the target region, e.g., `ap-south-1/execute-api/aws4_request`) and API Gateway does NOT support multi-region `SigV4a`, so when Route 53 latency/failover routing sends a request signed for `ap-south-1` to `eu-west-1`, authentication fails—use region-agnostic auth (JWT/Cognito/Lambda authorizer or mTLS) or client-side re-signing on failure; also, while DNS TTL is 60s, real-world Route 53 DNS failover takes 3–10 minutes due to client/JVM DNS caching (use Global Accelerator or CloudFront origin failover for sub-minute failover, and use geo-based routing when GDPR data residency applies); (2) Route 53 health checkers run on the public internet and cannot reach Private API endpoints, so Private APIs require CloudWatch alarm-based Route 53 health checks (`5XXError`, NLB `UnHealthyHostCount`); and (3) Map the governance controls across Preventative SCPs (`apigateway:Request/SecurityPolicy`, `apigateway:Request/AccessLoggingDestination`—noting the `StringLikeIfExists` caveat on stage updates—and `apigateway:Request/EndpointType`), Proactive CloudFormation Hooks / Guard rules, and Detective AWS Config managed rules (`api-gw-xray-enabled`, `api-gw-associated-with-waf`, `api-gw-execution-logging-enabled`, `api-gw-ssl-enabled`, `api-gw-endpoint-type-check`).
expectations: Activates the api-gateway skill and explains that SigV4 signatures are bound to a single AWS region and API Gateway does not support SigV4a (causing cross-region routed requests to fail), and notes that real-world Route 53 DNS failover takes 3–10 minutes due to client DNS caching
Explains that public Route 53 HTTP health checks cannot reach Private REST APIs, requiring CloudWatch alarm-based health checks instead

Maps organization-wide API governance across Preventative SCPs (`apigateway:Request/*` and `apigateway:Resource/*` condition keys), Proactive CloudFormation Hooks / Guard rules, and Detective AWS Config rules (`api-gw-xray-enabled`, `api-gw-associated-with-waf`, `api-gw-execution-logging-enabled`)
